chapter_reading.assessment: Literary correspondences with LAB and Esther suggest Judith circulated in Hebrew, but do not establish its original language or a surviving lost manuscript.
Ritual reading of Razis narrative; temple defilement and body symbolism are literary interpretations, not an archaeological location or trace.
Rajak disputes a lone-reader inference using4Maccabees and medievalYosippon; uncertain provenance/date and eight-century transmission gap retained.
Translation traditions and lost Hebrew1Maccabees discussed. Hebrew Vorlage and transmission loss are inference/attestation questions, not fresh field evidence.
Hypothetica reassignment to an anonymous Palestinian Jewish rationalist is argued from diction, deictic reference and priestly vow practices; Philo attribution remains scholarly dispute.
Historical authors’ condemnations of same-sex acts and Paul/Wisdom literary dependence analyzed. Polemical generalizations do not establish actual group conduct or archaeological controls.

Mason separates interpretation of Josephus from historical explanation, challenges a unified Zealot movement and Hebrew-name assumptions, and stresses that uncertain source labels are not established group membership. His alternative name reconstructions and troop-number adjustments remain hypotheses, not new field observations.

Segal argues Josephus used Hebrew/Aramaic proto-MT Daniel and retold historical prophecy selectively. Calendar calculations are exegetical reconstructions, not independent dates; Greek-source counterarguments and alternative explanations retained.

Sharon argues ContraApionem qualifies territory and emphasizes laws/Diaspora. Interpretive disagreement with Barclay and genre/audience alternatives remain explicit; not a reconstruction of physical boundaries.

Sterling infers constitution section was an afterthought and probably a second edition from transitions, textual variants and vocabulary. Authorial inconsistency and alternative readings are retained; no newly recovered manuscript or independent field evidence.

Liebowitz compares Doris and Mariamme through Josephus/rabbinic narratives. Ethnic identity, dates, motives and psychological reconstructions are disputed. A reconstructed ossuary name (printed243n26) has uncertain findspot and alternative male-nickname reading; not a firm identity proof. Bibliography printed260 mentions Schalit1963 Masada roundstructure/Mariamme tomb as a lead, without presenting excavation evidence.

Frey interprets James execution account as evidence of social respect and Pharisaic opposition to Ananus. Josephus does not name the others/protesters, and identifying them remains inference. High-priestly archive preservation is a secondary conjecture in printed272n41, not recovered archival evidence.

Ben-Yishai reads tyrant language as aristocratic betrayal and Roman literary trope. He proposes unburied bodies and melted temple vessels in Josephus were invented (printed289–290); that is an interpretive assertion, not new archaeological evidence of absence. Contrasts with chapter7 require preserving author disagreement.

Fishman-Duker distinguishes direct Josephus reception from derivative chains in Byzantine chronicles. Temple loot and tomb-plunder variants conflict across these sources (printed 301–304); relocations of Temple and Jericho geography (printed 312) cannot support dates or independent observations. Timotheus I cave manuscript report near Jericho c.800 (printed 307 and n.62) is a late derivative textual lead, not a recovered target or transmission proof.

Collins defends Hecataean attribution of Diodorus 40.3 against Schwartz/Gmirkin, while distinguishing Jewish Pseudo-Hecataeus. Attribution and textual dependence remain debated. Even accepting c.300 BCE testimony establishes only a form of Mosaic law, not the complete Pentateuch or a physical field finding.

Gruen reconsiders the blood and leper libels through fragmentary literary transmission and Josephus’s polemical selection. Claims about rarity, motives and social impact are the author’s interpretation; absence from surviving texts does not provide archaeological evidence of absence. Uncertain attribution and possible shared sources remain explicit.

Berthelot distinguishes disputed letter authenticity from a possible Judeo-Spartan relationship and compares ancestral territory narratives. She expressly does not infer literary influence from mythic similarities (printed 371). Kinship reconstruction and territorial rights are ancient ideological claims, not physical boundary observations.

Dov Gera argues 2 Maccabees treats Gerizim’s people as fellow Jews and hospitable; linguistic and narrative reading remains contested. He rejects harmonizing emendations motivated by Josephus’s divergent account (printed 384–386); temple names, dates and legal distinctions are textual inference, with coin-title chronology disagreements retained in printed 384 n.24.

Cohen separates Chrysostom’s hostile rhetoric from reconstructed Christian self-understanding. Ritual baths could reflect biblical caricature or contemporary practice (printed 399 n.13); Matrona grotto’s synagogue identity remains disputed (printed 402 n.26). Peaceful relations inferred from double silence (printed 398) and entertainment motives reconstructed (printed 407) are author inferences, not independent archaeological findings.

Bloch traces an unnamed bust from the Borghese collection (1832 attestation; excavation origin unknown) through unsupported identity captions. Similarity, racist physiognomy and repeated publication do not identify Josephus. The same coin is drawn differently in Eisler and Madden (printed 429 figs.20.7–8); preserve representation lineage. Internal narrative dates differ: Eisler’s Copenhagen visit 1929 at printed 427, but 1925 at printed 436; no silent harmonization.

Piotrkowski examines Willrich’s antisemitism and unsupported reconstructions of Herod. He distinguishes source criticism’s valid questions from prejudiced conclusions; bibliography is not fresh field evidence. Internal chronology problem: a 1925 project is said to receive help from August Wilmanns (1833–1917) at printed 454–455, left unresolved rather than repaired.

Goodman analyzes a nineteenth-century anonymous sequel and its probable D’Israeli-family authorship. Multiple citations and unacknowledged translation often reuse one earlier history (printed 476–479); reception and audience are inferred, not independent corroboration of ancient events. Uncertain authorship and edition dating remain explicit.

Price distinguishes recovered inscriptions from inferred unpreserved writing. Warning plaques were recovered through reuse rather than destruction deposits (printed 491–492). Matitya fragment’s original Temple location and dedication restoration remain uncertain (494–495); Bar Giora linkage is poorly justified (496); lost Herodian inscription destruction is explicitly conjectural (498–499). These are documentary survival controls, not target evidence.

Arubas and Leibner propose six previously unrecognized Second Temple synagogues from fragmentary remains and architecture. Wadi Hamam and recent Arbel work include fresh field observations; Capernaum, Gush Halav, Hammath and Merot reassess inherited campaigns and must be deduplicated. Synagogue identity and continuity remain inferential. Merot bath deposits are unsealed and complex remained accessible into medieval times (printed 535 n.56), so not secure construction-date contexts. All phase diagrams, captions and bibliography read.

Gafni contrasts solidarity images and threats with actual cross-regional assistance. Claudian papyrus preserved at Philadelphia (printed 565) has competing interpretations; speeches and Josephus variants do not prove coordinated military action. Lack of decisive evidence for collective Diaspora-revolt organization (printed 568) and Bar Kokhba aid (569) remains an evidentiary limitation, not physical proof of absence.

Tal Ilan interprets Herodian pigeon legend with Greek wordplay and a hypothesized shared Samias source. Rav Kahana could not have witnessed Herod’s reign (printed 578–579); first-person formula is literary marvel, not field eyewitness evidence. Manuscript variants, anonymous redaction and competing Sasanian-prototype interpretation remain explicit.

Brody analyzes rabbinic recognition of priestly privileges, competing genealogical standards and scholarly authority. Court, lineage and archive mentions are literary legal traditions rather than newly recovered institutional archives. Variants, uncertain dates of practices and different rabbinic responses retained.

Oppenheimer argues continued Jewish land ownership after revolts from Josephus and rabbinic law. Critical translation discrepancy preserved: editor’s printed 591 n.5 clarifies Isaac intended sell rather than release, while the displayed translation and ensuing inference at printed 592 use release. Legal prescriptions, legendary cases and inherited literary reports do not provide measured ownership shares or archaeological boundaries.

Schremer distinguishes attestation of sectarian disagreement from reliability of opponents’ attributed arguments. Reconstructs incense controversy from textual variants and possible rhetorical suppression; explicitly concedes substantial conjecture because no external source preserves the opponents’ reasons (printed 620). No direct archaeological observation or independent restored source.

Irshai proposes Antiochene disappointments helped trigger Julian’s Jerusalem program. Motives and causal timing are historical interpretation; authenticity of letter contested, temple vs city wording distinguished (printed 627 nn.3–5). Maayan Baruch restorer-of-temples inscription is inherited published evidence, not new excavation (629 n.12). Different fire narratives and later mythic expansion remain separate; no physical mechanism or recovered site proof.

McCollough locates Qana’s public building in the northwest quadrant of the acropolis at printed 81 and in the southwest quadrant at printed 86. This internal discrepancy remains unresolved. Ben David gives Ilan’s inventory as 180 at printed 177/table 1 but 187 at printed 180, and early Roman synagogue totals as ten in the introduction/table/conclusion but twelve at printed 184. Table 1’s 1993 row gives 77 sites, 58 survey and 26 excavation (84 combined). The 2016 table lists eight Samaritan sites while printed 178 says seven; printed 178’s 10 early Roman + 58 later Jewish + 7 Samaritan breakdown totals 75 against 74 excavated. Magness printed 171 describes turning 360 degrees from the entrance to face Jerusalem. This angle is internally problematic as a direction reversal; it remains a printed statement, not a measured movement or datum.

evidence.observation: Yodefat survey distinguishes square cistern opening with spiral steps, square opening with two or three steps and standing space, and bell-shaped cisterns. First type concentrated within upper wall; third distributed over site.
evidence.author_interpretation: Types and coin distributions are used to infer downhill growth of the settlement.
evidence.project_inference: Add morphological controls; opening/step form alone does not date a feature.
evidence.lineage: Yodefat 1992–1997 excavations/survey; Aviam 2005 dissertation and 1997 preliminary report, not independent new corroboration.

evidence.observation: Printed coin percentages for lowest plateau areasIII/VI are 12%,10.5%,37%,59%.
evidence.author_interpretation: Distribution is used to infer settlement expansion.
evidence.project_inference: Sum is 118.5%; preserve source values and flag inconsistency before numerical reuse.

evidence.observation: Yodefat agricultural survey found many open-land cisterns, no natural spring, two winepresses, one with Byzantine plaster. Gamla 27 silver coins near olive press reported without detailed sealed context here.
evidence.author_interpretation: Cisterns served herds; wool production and oil production diversified economy.
evidence.project_inference: Cistern husbandry function is interpretation; silver group is derivative pointer, requires original context before hoard inventory integration.

evidence.observation: Two Yodefat cisterns contained collected/disarticulated bones behind low walls; first man/woman/child, second about 20 individuals mainly children; enclosing debris no later than first centuryCE reported.
evidence.author_interpretation: Emergency reburial after siege 67 CE, perhaps one or two years later; attribution of Roman burial prohibition inferred.
evidence.project_inference: Cistern-to-burial reuse control; gathered bones and enclosing fill date distinguish from original water installation construction.

evidence.observation: Sepphoris crushed-limestone street below stonepaving contained Hellenistic/EarlyRoman sherds and Archelaeus coin; coin 119–120 CE directly beneath stone pavers.
evidence.author_interpretation: Firstcentury street route/planning preceded secondcentury monumental paving; theater founding date disputed across essays.
evidence.project_inference: Road alignment and visible paving require separate phases; same field observations do not supply two independent chronological confirmations.

evidence.observation: Qana northern stepped pool plaster dates 160 BCE–78 CE and 23–214 CE from different fractions. Large buildings mortar/plaster 4–234 CE 95% range. Southeastern chambers: small 1.10 mheight,2.10 mdepth,1.70 mwidth with 5 steps; larger 1.95 mheight,2.87 mdepth,1.77 mwidth about 3 m downslope, plaster 4–234 CE.
evidence.author_interpretation: Ritual baths and liquid industry proposed; firstdecadesfirst century founding inferred from combination of radiocarbon and pottery.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve broad ranges and uncertain function; small covered stepped rooms have documented alternative contexts. No datum transferred to scroll target.

evidence.observation: Mattila distinguishes excavated access/closing mechanisms from inferred household units and reconstructs Insula 2 phase changes. Glassware dating changed between Loffreda 1984 (latefirst/earlysecondCE) and 2002 (no later FirstWar).
evidence.author_interpretation: Houses became smaller over time and occupants could possess wealth above subsistence.
evidence.project_inference: Record edition-dependent chronology and modernpathway excavation gaps; reconstructed upperstories/households are not measured ancient datums.

evidence.observation: Oakman calls tunnels produceconcealment but n 44 records Aviam uncertainty. Different essays reuse Syon coin counts and Yodefat/Gamla campaign data. Fiensy notes broaddate burial samples and calls models working hypotheses.
evidence.author_interpretation: Authors disagree on economic and political organization.
evidence.project_inference: Undergroundtaxconcealment is hypothesis; bibliography and number of essays add no independent field evidence.

evidence.observation: Chronological typology is explicitly challenged in the introductory synthesis.
evidence.author_interpretation: The editor calls for individual building context rather than assuming architecture fixes date.
evidence.project_inference: Retain architecture as a morphological description; do not substitute it for stratigraphy.
evidence.lineage: Editorial synthesis, not a new field campaign.

evidence.observation: Masada rear room yielded two pits containing biblical scroll fragments at their bottoms; the pits were cut through the upper room floor. Greek and paleo-Hebrew symbols occur under personal names on ostraca.
evidence.author_interpretation: Yadin proposes a sacred-text depository but also considers concealment before destruction; symbol purpose remains uncertain.
evidence.project_inference: Track cuts, floors and deposits separately; emergency concealment is an alternative explanation, not an established purpose. This is contextual material and does not restart the parked initials test.
evidence.lineage: Masada 1963–1965 excavation lineage; duplicate later descriptions do not create separate observations.

evidence.observation: Masada hall is approximately 12×15 m; Herodium hall 10.5×15 m. Herodium bases rest on earth about 10 cm above an earlier floor, without a continuous stylobate; a bath adjoins the east wall.
evidence.author_interpretation: Foerster discusses conversion of existing Herodian halls and reconstructs architectural parallels.
evidence.project_inference: Separate earlier floor, conversion and later furnishings; the restored plans are not direct measurements of hidden geometry.
evidence.lineage: Abridged reprint of Foerster Eretz-Israel 11(1973),224–228; same excavations as later syntheses.

evidence.observation: Gamla has an aqueduct branch through the town wall, a depression collecting water, and a west channel connecting doorway and bath. Main threshold is flush with the floor and 1.5 m wide; a 0.9 m side threshold is about 1 m higher.
evidence.author_interpretation: Gutman and Ma‘oz give differing phase/orientation interpretations; Ma‘oz assigns the eastern basin/channel to revolt alteration and explains orientation by topography.
evidence.project_inference: Access height and hydraulic phase are useful controls. Multiple essays from one campaign are not independent corroboration.
evidence.lineage: Gamla campaign directed by Gutman; Ma‘oz architectural analysis shares field observations.

evidence.observation: Capernaum reports include mortar-embedded coins, older pavements, foundation fill, blocked drainage and coin groups of 2920 and more than 6000; section drawing shows distinct fills and floors.
evidence.author_interpretation: Loffreda proposes late construction; Foerster and Avi-Yonah dispute links between deposits, repairs and initial building.
evidence.project_inference: Encode each dated material with its depositional relation. Three disputing authors reviewing one campaign do not supply three independent dates.
evidence.lineage: Franciscan Capernaum 1968–1972 excavation lineage; earlier Kohl/Watzinger and Orfali work discussed.

evidence.observation: Hammath-Tiberias thresholds are destroyed; wall recesses suggest former openings. A strong box was set into a floor. Later cisterns west of the apse were converted into dwelling chambers.
evidence.author_interpretation: Dothan reconstructs door positions and assigns later alterations to LevelIA.
evidence.project_inference: Door locations are reconstructed; cistern conversion is a later reuse control, not a first-century feature.
evidence.lineage: Dothan excavation beginning 1961; phase relations within same site.

evidence.observation: Horvat Shema room under stairs yielded no significant artifacts; an earlier cave/tomb precedes the building.
evidence.author_interpretation: Identification as genizah is explicitly conjectural. Destruction dates depend partly on matching archaeological evidence to earthquake catalogues.
evidence.project_inference: Do not enter a confirmed cache or sacred-text store from the label alone; separate observed destruction from event-date attribution.
evidence.lineage: Shema 1970–1972 excavations; AASOR 42(1976) lineage.

evidence.observation: Gush Halav western corridor held 1943 coins in a pot attributed mostly to StratumVII. South doorway is 1.7 m wide with post and bolt holes; northwest doorway is 1.15 m wide with four steps down to the north.
evidence.author_interpretation: Meyers links the hoard to final use in the mid-sixth century and describes storage use of the western corridor.
evidence.project_inference: Useful access and late storage controls; do not promote this deposit into First Revolt evidence. Native small bema dimensions are 1.46×1.7×0.3 m, correcting OCR 3 m.
evidence.lineage: Gush Halav 1977–1978 campaign; distinguish earlier Hamburger 1954 hoard.

evidence.observation: Beth-Shean east room contained a deep pit cleared to about 7 m. Nearby Greek inscription relates digging to two superintendents whose names are unclear. A coin in north doorway blocking belongs to the Umayyad period.
evidence.author_interpretation: Bahat considers later reuse and alterations of the complex.
evidence.project_inference: Pit depth is cleared depth, not total measured depth. The blocked doorway coin dates blocking, not initial entrance construction.
evidence.lineage: Bahat 1970–1971 excavation; House of Leontis earlier Zori campaign separately referenced.

evidence.observation: Ma‘oz Hayim cubicle behind bema contained lamps, coins and glass and was paved with reused roof tiles. About 50 coins outside the south wall were wrapped in cloth within a broken roof tile.
evidence.author_interpretation: Cubicle was probably a genizah; hoard probably hidden in an emergency.
evidence.project_inference: Both functional labels remain author hypotheses; original records needed before a sealed-context hoard assertion.
evidence.lineage: Tzaferis 1974 excavation campaign.

evidence.observation: Rehob land preparation disturbed a clay box holding 27 Byzantine gold coins. Three north thresholds and one east threshold survived. Earlier sculptural fragments were reused.
evidence.author_interpretation: Vitto suggests a synagogue hoard and possible earlier building, and identifies settlement by literary and place-name tradition.
evidence.project_inference: Disturbed discovery is not a sealed deposit; reused sculpture does not establish an earlier synagogue; site-name identification remains inferential.
evidence.lineage: Rehob 1973 onward excavation; original coins discovered during 1969 land preparation.

evidence.observation: En-Gedi narthex has a laver; charred scroll traces and dark material were found near the niche. Earlier doorway was blocked to form a niche. At Eshtemoa a bedrock cave had not been cleared.
evidence.author_interpretation: Earlier space behind the En-Gedi niche later used for storage or genizah; dark mass probably a codex.
evidence.project_inference: Track direct burned material separately from proposed object/function. Eshtemoa cave remains an explicitly unexamined feature.
evidence.lineage: En-Gedi 1970–1971 and Eshtemoa 1969 onward campaigns, separate observations.

evidence.observation: Susiya courtyard is 1.5 m below hall; floor openings lead to a rainwater cistern and series of caves. Honorius coin was found below first-phase narthex mosaic.
evidence.author_interpretation: Caves possibly former quarry used as stores; mosque dating inferred from finds and style.
evidence.project_inference: A coin below pavement constrains the pavement phase; it does not date every cave or the whole building.
evidence.lineage: Susiya 1969–1972 campaign; earlier survey lineage explicit.

evidence.observation: En-Gedi inscription includes a prohibition against revealing the town secret. Differences of script and wording are described.
evidence.author_interpretation: Several competing explanations are discussed: guild/trade secret, balsam production, political allegiance, religious oath and scriptures.
evidence.project_inference: The inscription alone does not choose among explanations. Script differences alone do not prove a later construction phase.
evidence.lineage: Levine interpretation of same En-Gedi mosaic; not independent field evidence.

evidence.observation: Rehob inscription preserves agricultural rules, place names and gates; some text is otherwise unattested.
evidence.author_interpretation: Sussmann dates composition after Palestinian Talmud and suggests fifth century at earliest, possibly as late as seventh from site finds.
evidence.project_inference: Useful ancient toponym corpus with dating uncertainty; legal boundaries are not a direct map of a first-century itinerary.
evidence.lineage: Same Rehob mosaic as Vitto field report; text analysis not new site observation.

evidence.observation: Dabbura lintels and fragments and Tiberias inscriptions survive in reused or uncertain original settings; marble profiles affect fragment identification.
evidence.author_interpretation: Dabbura school inscription is linked to named sage; Tiberias funerary restorations are rejected in favour of basin/lintel donations.
evidence.project_inference: Personal identification and reconstructed function require uncertainty labels; names do not replace sealed archaeological dating.
evidence.lineage: Dabbura 1967 survey and Urman 1972; Tiberias fragments reviewed from Schwabe 1947 and Landau oral report.

evidence.observation: Diaspora survey includes disputed identifications and reused architecture. Delos lamps have pagan motifs. Stobi basilica previously identified as synagogue is a church over earlier buildings.
evidence.author_interpretation: Foerster distinguishes identification arguments and revisions; Dura religious and social uses are reconstructed.
evidence.project_inference: Iconographic resemblance and reused columns cannot by themselves fix building function/date. These are background controls outside local target scoring.
evidence.lineage: Survey of separately cited campaigns; Dura excavation/fresco literature shares one archaeological source.

evidence.observation: Sardis marble plaque was found outside a door and may have been moved. Basin on tall pedestal is not connected to water pipes; forecourt fountain is separate. Furnishings intrude into earlier mosaic in different phases.
evidence.author_interpretation: Seager considers multiple uses of main hall and identifies probable Torah shrines.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve findspot uncertainty, hydraulic distinction and phase sequence; present display location does not establish ancient provenance.
evidence.lineage: Harvard/Cornell Sardis excavations beginning 1962; architectural analysis 1972 lineage.

evidence.observation: Corinth capital and synagogue inscription lack direct contextual link. Mopsuestia mosaics include Noah and Samson scenes, repairs and a small bronze cross.
evidence.author_interpretation: Corinth finds probably share a period; Mopsuestia church/synagogue identification and artistic genealogy are argued from iconography and parallels.
evidence.project_inference: Record uncertain building attribution; motif resemblance and narrative sequence do not establish independent territorial or chronological controls.
evidence.lineage: Corinth Scranton 1957; Mopsuestia Budde 1955 excavation and later artistic analyses.

evidence.observation: The chapter describes two Greek Temple warning plaques: a complete copy found north of the Old City and published in 1871, later reappearing in Istanbul, and a fragment found in 1935 in secondary use in a tomb near Lions Gate. Their hands and minor variants differ; no Latin copy is reported as recovered.
evidence.author_interpretation: The author compares their wording and Josephus’s accounts and proposes a common exemplar.
evidence.project_inference: Keep findspot, secondary context and original installation separate. The two stones and literary descriptions do not identify a scroll landmark.
evidence.lineage: CIIP I.1 no. 2 and inherited Clermont-Ganneau/Iliffe discoveries; a modern synthesis of the same finds.

evidence.observation: The chapter reviews a fragmentary Matitya limestone plaque in southern destruction debris, an informal Bar Gio[...] inscription beneath fallen Robinson’s Arch, and an inscribed Yehosef vessel and qorban/bird handle west of the Temple Mount.
evidence.author_interpretation: Dedication restoration and original placement are uncertain. The author rejects an unsupported Bar Giora association and discusses ritual-vessel functions.
evidence.project_inference: Keep incomplete readings, object functions and original locations conditional. Destruction debris and a secondary findspot alone cannot locate the original inscription.
evidence.lineage: CIIP I.1 nos. 4–8 and inherited published observations; no new independent find from this essay.

evidence.observation: The Nicanor ossuary inscription was recovered in 1902. The proposed bronze-gate inscription is not extant. The chapter reports Herod’s name on domestic objects but no monumental inscription from his realm.
evidence.author_interpretation: Nicanor’s identity and parsing are conditional. The author presents spontaneous damnatio memoriae as a guess, with destruction or reuse as other possible explanations.
evidence.project_inference: A missing inscription is a hypothesis, and its absence cannot establish suppression or a particular target location.
evidence.lineage: CIIP I.98 and inherited epigraphic corpus; proposed lost objects are not additional archaeological observations.

evidence.observation: Wadi Hamam soundings beneath the mosaic yielded 559 identifiable rims, 92% Early Roman or earlier, with later sherds limited to bedding or disturbances. Seventeen coins include Tiberius (17–24 CE) and Agrippa I (37–43 CE). The western annex has four rooms with benches and plaster floors, ash deposits 20–60 cm thick in southern rooms, and an 11-coin group ending with Hadrian. A possible table base measures 0.6 × 0.8 m and survives 30 cm high.
evidence.author_interpretation: The author dates the terrace to the mid-first century CE and destruction to 125–135 CE, while interpreting the early building as a synagogue and relating destruction to revolt.
evidence.project_inference: Distinguish observed assemblages and room deposits from building identity and village-wide causal attribution. The possible table function is uncertain; campaign and final-report repetition provide one source family.
evidence.lineage: Author-directed Wadi Hamam excavation and Leibner 2018 final report; the 2024 essay reuses those campaign observations.

evidence.observation: Arbel’s new excavations from 2012 exposed low platforms about 2 m long and 45 cm wide, chalk floors and first-century BCE/CE phases cut by later colonnade foundations. Figure 24.7 labels an arch as leading to a miqveh with a question mark.
evidence.author_interpretation: An early synagogue is considered probable from a partial public-building plan. The end date is unresolved, and wall 3A16 could belong to an earlier phase.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve partial exposure, queried water-installation identification and alternative wall phasing. Avoid forcing the early walls into a later plan.
evidence.lineage: Recent author-directed Arbel campaign, distinct from Kohl/Watzinger 1905 and 1987–1989 clearing; its derived figures are the same campaign.

evidence.observation: At Capernaum, a basalt pebble floor is reported 1.8 m below the nave, exposed for at least 8 × 20 m. Basalt outer walls differ in orientation and are 130 cm wide compared with 70 cm limestone walls. Stucco beneath the alley and reused basalt are discussed. Gush Halav’s proposed predecessor has limited exposure with frescoes and a capital.
evidence.author_interpretation: Corbo assigns the basalt building to the first century; Loffreda favors the second–fourth centuries for the walls and first century for the pebble floor. Early building identity remains inferential. The Gush Halav plastered pool is described agriculturally, with ritual-bath use as an unsupported alternative.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve floor, walls and later building as separate phased observations, and retain the dating disagreement. Alternative pool function is not a confirmed ritual datum.
evidence.lineage: Corbo/Loffreda and Meyers campaigns also encountered in Sources 29 and 10; stylistic reinterpretation adds no new excavation.

evidence.observation: Hammath Stratum III includes a partly exposed hall about 11 × 16 m beneath later synagogues. The essay notes that some reconstructed annexes are speculative.
evidence.author_interpretation: Dothan’s palaestra/gymnasium interpretation competes with a possible synagogue interpretation. The 132–135 CE destruction date is inherited from Dothan.
evidence.project_inference: Keep excavated extent, reconstructed annexes, function and attributed destruction chronology separate.
evidence.lineage: Dothan’s 1960s campaign, already in Source 29; the newer essay interprets the same record.

evidence.observation: At Merot, the essay notes the absence of a final report, reused column drums with Greek and alef marks, and six connected underground hewn spaces including a bath and cistern used into the Middle Ages. Figure 24.23 shows a rear breach. Note 56 places late-fourth-century pottery chiefly in bath locus 90 rather than beneath a sealed floor.
evidence.author_interpretation: An early building and synagogue identity are inferred cumulatively. Continued rear access weakens use of the bath pottery as a construction date.
evidence.project_inference: Bath, cistern, access and reuse need phase-controlled documentation. Unsealed pottery and later access cannot supply a secure founding datum.
evidence.lineage: Ilan/Damati 1980s excavation and archive reinterpretation; no independent field campaign from the later essay.

evidence.observation: Notes acknowledge Gamla as a basilical exception, report an earlier Umm al-Qanatir building detected after 40% of floors were lifted, and discuss 12 reused Doric capitals in the En Gedi bathhouse and a possible reference in P.Yadin 19 (128 CE).
evidence.author_interpretation: The authors propose continuity of synagogue sanctity and public property. The En Gedi predecessor remains unexcavated and its papyrus association is possible.
evidence.project_inference: Record these as publication and excavation leads with their qualifications. Reused capitals and a possible papyrus name do not establish a located early synagogue.
evidence.lineage: Inherited Gamla, Umm al-Qanatir and En Gedi observations and textual interpretation; forthcoming work is an access lead.

evidence.observation: Noga-Banai describes Daniel in a Christian painted tomb found near Loḥamei HaGetaot in1971 and in the damaged sixth-century Naaran synagogue mosaic found1918. Naaran fragments had formerly been combined into one menorah; museum conservation in1998 separated the parts and restored one original design. The tomb’s late-fourth/early-fifth-century dating, medium and setting differ from the synagogue.
evidence.author_interpretation: The author associates paired lights with cyclic time and Daniel with resurrection and eschatology. Christian artists at Naaran are a possibility from shared visual formulas; the author leaves unexplained why the Galilee tomb combination is otherwise exceptional.
evidence.project_inference: The conserved menorah image is a documented restoration. Shared motifs and theological readings cannot establish an artisan identity, hidden cache or a first-century landscape relation. Preserve the tomb’s Christian attribution and late-antique dates.
evidence.lineage: Published tomb/synagogue observations and museum-conservation history; iconographic comparison does not add an independent excavation.

evidence.observation: Native illustrations include a Daniel painting in a tomb near Kibbutz Loḥamei HaGetaot (35.1), L.-H. Vincent’s Naaran mosaic drawing with a metric scale (35.2) and its cabinet/menorah detail (35.3), the Sepphoris decorative-floor drawing (35.4), Carthage mosaic drawing and a Roman personification photograph (35.5a–b), a restored Naaran menorah panel (35.6), and a circular mosaic detail from Ḥazor-Ashdod (35.7). Restored and missing portions are visible in the Naaran panel.
evidence.author_interpretation: Noga-Banai argues that Daniel, paired lights and cyclic-time imagery express eschatological hopes, individually in the Christian tomb and collectively in the synagogue. Shared decorative formulas and possible Christian artists are interpretive proposals.
evidence.project_inference: Record restored decoration separately from surviving tesserae and architectural geometry. Cross-site iconographic resemblance adds no independent location or deposit evidence.
evidence.lineage: Museum, archival drawing and excavation-image reproductions; private inspection only.

evidence.observation: Weiss records the first Magdala stone on the hall floor in the final building debris, with first-phase installation and original position unresolved. Kur stone was reused in a bench around600CE; Hamam fragment came from alley collapse above a third-century street. A fourth/fifth-century coin may make the proposed late-third-century collapse date too early. Second Magdala stone lacks precise findspot/context. Kanaf and Deir Aziz table pieces were reused. The printed716 table gives Magdala1 width55cm versus57cm in p700 prose, and Kanaf width60/height42cm versus66/24cm in p714 prose.
evidence.author_interpretation: Weiss proposes stone tables rested scrolls between standing readings and survived into later Roman/Byzantine synagogues. He rejects applying all such pieces to First Temple-period predecessors. Building/storage functions, original stone uses and later replacement by taller furniture are argued reconstructions; some site/date disagreements remain explicit.
evidence.project_inference: Keep measured/reported dimensions, secondary contexts, the author’s functions and project inference separate. The internal dimension discrepancies require the original field reports before metric use. A translated revision of JRA34(2021),608–631 shares observations with that paper and existing site reports; count each field campaign once.
evidence.lineage: Translated revision of the author’s2021JRA paper; inherited Magdala, Kur, Hamam, Kanaf and Deir Aziz field observations and informant contributions.

evidence.observation: Native illustrations show the first Magdala stone photograph (34.1), the Dura-Europos reading painting (34.2), an artistic reconstruction of a Magdala Torah-reading scene (34.3), two faces of the Kur stone (34.4a–b), Hamam stone fragment photograph and drawing (34.5), four faces of the second Magdala stone with a 0–30 cm scale (34.6), and reused stone pieces at Kanaf and Deir Aziz (34.7–8).
evidence.author_interpretation: The reading scene is an artistic reconstruction proposal. Weiss interprets low stone tables as rests for scrolls before, between and after standing readings, and rejects several competing reconstructions.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve the difference between source photographs, drawings and artistic reconstructions. Reused table pieces cannot independently date their first use. These inspected figures have not been digitized into target geometry.
evidence.lineage: Published illustrations from named excavation/museum sources; the project inspected the native reproductions, not the original objects.

evidence.observation: Ben-Eliyahu contrasts world descriptions in the Genesis Apocryphon, Jubilees and Josephus with geographically narrower rabbinic references. The chapter compares Ionian three-part geography and Babylonian/Enochic sevenfold patterns; notes identify disagreements over eight versus seven outer regions and the absence of a surrounding ocean in Enoch.
evidence.author_interpretation: He proposes that the decline of Jewish participation as an independent political actor explains the retreat of comprehensive world geography and distant diaspora references after the Bar Kokhba revolt. This is offered as an initial explanatory study.
evidence.project_inference: Distinguish ideological world descriptions, legal territorial bounds and physical maps. Similar numerical schemes cannot alone establish common dependence or a measured landscape. The political explanation is author inference; source silence is not proof of absent communities or contacts.
evidence.lineage: Literary and historiographical comparison; no new archaeological survey. Earlier map and text interpretations are explicitly discussed.

evidence.observation: Hacham reviews traditions about Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, Gamaliel and Yavneh, including calendar regulation, prayer, Passover practice and requests for Roman permission. He distinguishes later attribution and literary patterns from securely dated evidence; the two soldiers story is explicitly treated as legendary.
evidence.author_interpretation: Hacham proposes that Yavneh leaders reduced practical dependence on the Temple and concentrated on religious authority to avoid political conflict with Rome. Roman recognition of a religious leadership is inferred. He acknowledges alternative explanations, incompatible traditions and the limits of a single model.
evidence.project_inference: This is a proposed historical explanation of transmitted texts, not direct evidence that a particular institution, treasure transfer or cache occupied a mapped archaeological feature. Retain the author’s conditional status for motives and Roman recognition.
evidence.lineage: Rabbinic texts and modern historical analysis; shares textual sources with earlier Yavneh syntheses.

evidence.observation: Mandel compares the Genesis Rabbah 33.1 and Leviticus Rabbah 27.1 introductions, including their manuscript variants, lexical substitutions and reordered stories. Alexander’s treasure dispute and the distant realm beyond dark mountains occur within a literary comparison.
evidence.author_interpretation: Mandel argues that Leviticus Rabbah reworked the Genesis Rabbah introduction, converting its treatment of theodicy and human moral responsibility into a national eschatological framework. He discusses contrary priority arguments and proposes further comparison of other passages.
evidence.project_inference: The treasure litigation and ideal distant realm are literary motifs. Neither supplies an excavated deposit, a survey datum, or a geographical identification. The chapter’s source-priority argument remains the author’s philological assessment.
evidence.lineage: Comparison of inherited rabbinic manuscript traditions and earlier scholarship; no new field observation.

evidence.observation: Editors review disputed chronology and architecture, and caution that the Kur stone survives in secondary use and lacks a known original context. The introductory survey discusses both late-antique construction and continuation into the early Islamic period. Magdala’s full report was still pending at the date of this 2021 volume.
evidence.author_interpretation: The editors advocate local material and reception contexts and criticize broad theological readings of decoration; Kur dining and liturgical interpretations are distinguished as competing proposals.
evidence.project_inference: Retain excavation lineage and source-date limits. Introductory summaries repeat field reports and are not independent observations. The Kur disagreement with Weiss 2024 in Source 58 must remain explicit.
evidence.lineage: Editorial synthesis of previously published campaigns and chapters, not a new excavation.

evidence.observation: The editors summarize the chapters and provide their cited-source bibliography. Their account distinguishes Spigel’s argument against widespread domestic worship from Bonnie’s proposed house-synagogue explanation, and reports competing iconographic readings of Japhi‘a and Beth Alpha.
evidence.author_interpretation: The volume presents competing explanations for chronology, gathering space and art rather than a single agreed model.
evidence.project_inference: Chapter summaries and bibliography are derivative pointers. Resolve claims in the relevant chapter and original excavation before using them as observations.
evidence.lineage: Helsinki 2016 conference proceedings, published 2021; editorial synthesis of the contributing essays.

evidence.observation: Runesson and Cirafesi distinguish civic assemblies from association gatherings. Their notes classify Qumran Loci 4, 30 and 77 functionally, compare Magdala’s gathering hall and market setting, and record disagreement over Nabratein: excavators propose a mid-second-century phase, Magness a mid-fourth-century terminus post quem, and Spigel argues that unpublished field records affect the disagreement. Qana’s cited mortar/plaster result is 4–235 CE.
evidence.author_interpretation: The authors favor continuity across 70 CE and regard the archaeological gap and contested chronologies as inadequate grounds for assigning later changes directly to the Temple’s destruction.
evidence.project_inference: Qumran association-synagogue and dining labels are scholarly interpretations. Published and unpublished records are different access scopes; retain the chronological disagreement and broad radiocarbon interval.
evidence.lineage: Inherited Qumran, Magdala, Qana and Meiron-project campaigns; Runesson, Binder, Meyers, Magness and Spigel syntheses add no independent excavation.

evidence.observation: The Qana shrine-like platform is reported as a late fifth- or sixth-century addition. Nabratein’s proposed shrine in its first phase is uncertain because the recovered pediment is assigned to phase 2a. Notes preserve alternative explanations for Umm el-‘Umdan’s northern bench form, dispute Magdala’s entrance reconstruction, and leave Delos identification and phase open. Qiryat Sepher and Umm el-‘Umdan are cited as buildings continuing across 70 CE.
evidence.author_interpretation: The authors argue that orientation and Temple-related decoration have pre-70 examples and cannot by themselves establish a post-70 architectural transformation.
evidence.project_inference: A platform does not establish a shrine without its phase and furnishing evidence. Orientation, doorway reconstruction and iconographic meanings require separate arguments; no source direction is transferred to a scroll target.
evidence.lineage: Qana, Nabratein, Umm el-‘Umdan, Qiryat Sepher, Gamla and Magdala published observations reused in a comparative historical argument.

evidence.observation: The essay samples leadership titles, Torah-reading and prayer texts, and judicial references, with notes and bibliography. Footnote 55 explicitly acknowledges the lack of direct evidence for Palestinian civic synagogues serving as treasuries, while mentioning diaspora parallels.
evidence.author_interpretation: The authors explain later synagogue change through rabbinic influence, Christian competition and loss of local self-government. Treasury use in Palestine is proposed as a possibility from diaspora analogy.
evidence.project_inference: Keep literary attestation, institutional reconstruction and archaeological evidence separate. The treasury analogy supplies no Palestinian cache observation or Copper Scroll location.
evidence.lineage: Literary-source and prior-scholarship synthesis; repeated reports and interpretive works do not multiply field evidence.

evidence.observation: Bonnie surveys the second–third-century gap, including disputed Nabratein deposits, Qana’s proposed early phase and alternative explanations based on rebuilding, house gatherings and revolt destruction. Notes preserve the objection that Nabratein’s sealed pottery can extend into the fourth century and the separate issue of unpublished excavation data.
evidence.author_interpretation: He argues that later rebuilding alone does not explain the chronological pattern and seeks a social explanation for the choice of monumental buildings.
evidence.project_inference: The gap depends on dating, identification and detection. Retain Magness’s terminus-post-quem objection separately from Spigel’s unpublished-data explanation; archaeological absence supplies no secure census or destruction attribution.
evidence.lineage: Levine, Tsafrir, Meyers/Magness/Spigel and Qana syntheses, drawing on inherited field campaigns already represented elsewhere in this ledger.

evidence.observation: Bonnie’s native figures include a regional map marking early certain/uncertain and post 70 CE synagogues, two phases of the Priene bouleuterion with 10 m scale, and a Gamla plan with 10 m scale, western miqveh L 1060, water channel, route arrows and entrance photo.
evidence.author_interpretation: Captioned modified plans and the author’s map serve an architectural comparison. Text on p 70 explicitly calls the Hasmonean political-association conjecture tentative and states that direct supporting archaeological/textual evidence is absent apart from locations.
evidence.project_inference: Keep mapped certainty classes and plan derivation. Arrows and comparative resemblance cannot establish function, construction chronology or an itinerary.
evidence.lineage: Bonnie map; modified Kockel Priene and Yavor Gamla plans plus author entrance photo.

evidence.observation: Bonnie compares early gathering buildings and Hellenistic bouleuteria. Note 47, citing Yavor, describes Gamla’s main entrance screened by contemporary service/storage rooms and reached through an L-shaped vestibule; the other entrance required a bent stair about 3 m high. He expressly calls the proposed Hasmonean connection tentative, with no direct archaeological or textual evidence beyond location, and rejects Netzer’s Jericho synagogue identification in favor of a peristyle house with garden triclinium. The chapter and cited-source bibliography end at printed 80.
evidence.author_interpretation: He proposes that lingering Hasmonean cultural influence motivated monumental synagogues and that later house gatherings could explain institutional continuity. He distinguishes local elites adopting traditions from direct sponsorship by Hasmonean kings.
evidence.project_inference: Access and sight-line arrangements are usable published architectural relations; political memories and the inferred shift to houses remain hypotheses. No current regional rarity denominator, treasury location or Copper Scroll association follows from this comparison.
evidence.lineage: Gamla/Yavor original architecture, earlier Priene and other bouleuterion studies, Netzer’s Jericho campaign and inherited early-synagogue reports. The modified plans and comparative essay reuse those observations.

evidence.observation: McCollough reports a roughly five-hectare early Roman Qana village, sixty cisterns and no located natural water source. He describes a possible courtyard ritual pool, a plastered rock-cut bell-shaped columbarium and southeastern plastered industrial installations beside two underground domed stepped spaces. Their function is uncertain. The introduction places the public building northwest on the acropolis, while the later description says southwest.
evidence.author_interpretation: He interprets differentiated houses and industrial areas as signs of village complexity; ritual bathing, flax processing and tanning are proposed functions for the stepped industrial structures.
evidence.project_inference: Cistern dependence and underground access forms are comparative observations within this excavation’s scope. Keep stepped form, plaster, possible ritual function and industrial use separate. Resolve the quadrant disagreement against the field plan before locating this building from prose.
evidence.lineage: University of Puget Sound Qana campaign begun by Douglas Edwards and continued by McCollough; earlier Richardson descriptions and repeated campaign photographs share that field lineage.

evidence.observation: Qana figures show a Lower Galilee road map, aerial view labelled reservoir/road?/acropolis/lower village, columbarium plan and section with scales, stepped industrial installation photograph, hall aerial/plan, column/base/capital photographs, and a western-wall foundation diagram with mortar/plaster radiocarbon ranges. Figure 9 labels CR 8 as 1900±45 BP/4–236 calAD, CR 12 B 1785±45 BP/128–382 calAD, and CR 5 A 1375±45 BP/602–763 calAD. Adjacent text records 60 cisterns, an uncertain function for underground stepped structures, and a reused capital.
evidence.author_interpretation: McCollough identifies the hall as synagogue, links foundation pottery and mortar radiocarbon to early construction, and regards possible industrial-area ritual baths as uncertain. Broad radiocarbon ranges are not single-year construction dates.
evidence.project_inference: The full chapter, notes and bibliography are now continuously read through printed 95; these native observations remain figure/caption-specific. Use original laboratory/context documentation before tighter chronology. Captioned building and functional labels remain excavator assessments.
evidence.lineage: University of Puget Sound Qana campaign; Edwards photographs, Söderlund drawing, Rosenberg map and Recht foundation drawing; overlap with earlier Source 10 Qana chapter.

evidence.observation: Qana’s hall is reported as approximately 20 × 15 m, with a 3 × 5 m northeastern room, southern entrance, 1.5 m western wall, plastered aisles and flattened-bedrock nave. A reused Ionic capital and column/stylobate fragments are described. Foundation-level mortar dates to 4–236 CE at 95% probability; earliest floor material dates to 128–382 CE; small sealed subfloor ceramic samples include a form beginning around 100 CE and a second-century jug form. The small room’s bench plaster dates to 100–300 CE, from a report intended for the final publication.
evidence.author_interpretation: The author favors late-first/early-second-century founding and mid-second-century elaboration, treating the assemblages as termini post quem. Orientation is additional support in his argument. The attached room could be a study room or storage for books or ritual objects.
evidence.project_inference: Broad radiocarbon intervals, residual foundation coin, few readable sherds, disturbed annex foundations and source-specific endpoints need separate records. The reported phase interpretation is narrower than each dating interval. Preserve 4–236 here and the earlier essay’s 4–235 without silently harmonizing them. Room function remains conditional.
evidence.lineage: Qana foundation, floor and annex observations from the same excavation; Rech et al. 2003 mortar study and an unpublished floor report provide analytical components, not independent buildings.

evidence.observation: Of twenty sampled Qana roof tiles, Shapiro assigned eleven to Cyprus or Cilicia; the petrology report was unpublished at the time. McCollough models a population around 1,200 and seats around 225–250, with seating assumptions stated. He describes Byzantine changes including a podium on the Jerusalem side. No dedication inscription identifies the building’s donors. Notes and the cited-source bibliography are read through printed 95; viewer 97 is blank.
evidence.author_interpretation: Imported materials and housing differences motivate an affluent, socially differentiated village interpretation. Restricted attendance, secular communal use, migration and priestly-course funding are alternative possibilities; the author leaves financing uncertain.
evidence.project_inference: Population, attendance and social composition are estimates and hypotheses. Preserve the tile sample denominator and unpublished analytical scope. A possible priestly migration or costly building does not establish the presence, source or destination of a treasury.
evidence.lineage: Qana excavation, Shapiro’s 1998–2001 tile sample, Spigel’s capacity methodology and inherited Qalir/priestly-course literature; village-model outputs are derived from those inputs.

evidence.observation: Grey surveys priestly leadership and Torah-reading evidence from Pentateuchal legislation, Ezra/Nehemiah, Chronicles, Ben Sira, Josephus and sectarian rules. He explicitly distinguishes ideal constitutions from uncertain implementation and notes that pre-70 priestly residence in Galilee rests substantially on circumstantial evidence. The Damascus Document and Rule of the Community require priestly roles in local study and legal gatherings.
evidence.author_interpretation: He proposes that public and sectarian assemblies contributed to synagogue development and that priestly participation could continue across 70 CE. He recognizes local non-priestly leadership and variation.
evidence.project_inference: Normative texts and social reconstructions are literary evidence. References to assembly do not determine a particular excavated building, and priestly leadership does not locate a cache. The chapter is a synthesis of inherited sources rather than an additional field observation.
evidence.lineage: Ancient literary and rule texts interpreted through Runesson, Gillihan, Sanders and other prior scholarship; avoid counting each modern retelling as independent corroboration.

evidence.observation: Grey lists indirect priestly synagogue evidence at Tiberias, Magdala and Masada. Note 76 cites Masada ostraca found in or near the synagogue and Herodium documents concerning priestly gifts collected and distributed through a treasury; note 77 collects literary references to diaspora sacred funds. He discusses the Theodotos inscription as stronger evidence, while the precise building and public/private status remain uncertain. Notes 89–90 say the Jerusalem ossuary with Apamea/Palmyra synagogue functionaries is unprovenanced, with Silwan suggested by its editors. Essene/Qumran comparisons and the conclusion retain source and geographic limits.
evidence.author_interpretation: Priests are argued to have participated in some pre-70 synagogue leadership and liturgy, with continuity into later periods. Magdala priestly connections are explicitly speculative and later rabbinic rituals may be projected backward.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve in-building versus nearby ostracon context, textually mentioned treasury versus excavated feature, and diaspora versus Palestinian scope. These are useful original-source leads, not located Copper Scroll deposits. The unprovenanced ossuary supplies uncertain findspot evidence. Theodotos’s attested functions do not fix the associated building plan.
evidence.lineage: Masada final-report epigraphy, DJD II no. 24, Cave of Letters documents, CIIP I nos. 9 and 1119–1120, Josephus/Philo and inherited Magdala observations; each original object/corpus remains one source family.

evidence.observation: Grey’s cited-source bibliography includes the Masada final reports, Cave of Letters documents, CIIP volumes, Gordon’s Land and Temple, Gillihan’s comparative civic study and the prior synagogue-origin debate. Viewer 133 is a blank separating leaf.
evidence.author_interpretation: The bibliography documents the sources for the chapter’s historical synthesis.
evidence.project_inference: Bibliographic pointers are access leads. The chapters and notes are read; works merely cited have not thereby been inspected or independently verified.
evidence.lineage: Bibliography of the same Grey essay; no added field observation or independent corroboration.

evidence.observation: Ryan distinguishes public municipal assemblies from association synagogues and synagogue functionaries from town magistrates or councils. His examples come from Susanna, Ben Sira, Judith, Josephus’s Tiberias meetings and Gospel disputes. He notes uncertain Bethulia identification, fictional or anachronistic narrative settings, unequal influence within assemblies and the difference between a public presence and the whole population attending. Notes and cited-source bibliography are complete through printed 152; viewers 154–155 are a part divider and blank leaf.
evidence.author_interpretation: He argues that public opinion and reputation helped decide legal and political disputes even when local officials led proceedings, and interprets architectural resemblance to bouleuteria as compatible with shared functions.
evidence.project_inference: Literary representations, inferred institutional practice and excavated buildings remain separate evidence classes. The article supplies no located treasury, measured underground feature or new building observation. Public use does not imply universal simultaneous attendance.
evidence.lineage: Ancient narrative and normative texts, interpreted through Runesson, Binder, Levine, Korner and Ryan’s earlier work; inherited architecture and seating models are reused.

evidence.observation: Magness reviews traditional synagogue types and their revised chronology. She reports more than 25,000 bronze coins and pottery below Capernaum paving, with the latest finds around 500 CE. For the Jericho synagogue, nine early eighth-century coins came from a gap between the northwest-aisle wall and mosaic end. She separates this last-use context from construction. Galilean, broadhouse and apsidal buildings occur within overlapping late-antique periods.
evidence.author_interpretation: She dates Capernaum no earlier than the beginning of the sixth century, disputes an unsupported earlier rebuilding explanation, and treats the traditional linear architectural chronology as invalid. Jericho’s absence of figures is not dated by the last-use coins.
evidence.project_inference: Keep each published stratigraphic context and author’s dating argument distinct from stylistic classification. The Jericho coins alone cannot date initial construction or prove an iconoclastic origin. Capernaum’s upper gallery and shrine furniture in the descriptive synthesis include reconstructed features, whose evidentiary basis must be separately checked.
evidence.lineage: Franciscan Capernaum campaigns, Baramki’s Jericho report and inherited regional synagogue excavations; these are already represented through earlier source families.

evidence.observation: Magness describes Huqoq as about 20 × 15 m, with the nave floor 20 cm below the aisles. Her excavation scope includes most of the east aisle, northern half of the nave and a small west-aisle area. Probes under east-wall foundations and intact mosaic bedding found no immediately underlying earlier floor. A fourteenth–fifteenth-century public building reused and extended walls, raising the stylobate and pedestals about 1 m on reused synagogue fragments. Some reused column drums preserve painted plaster. Note 35 excludes the 2018–2019 discoveries from this article.
evidence.author_interpretation: She dates the synagogue no earlier than the beginning of the fifth century and treats Huqoq and Wadi Hamam as members of a regional mosaic-floored Galilean architectural group.
evidence.project_inference: Nave/aisle levels, raised medieval supports, ancient floors and reused painted fragments belong to different phases. The reported absence of an earlier floor is limited to the stated probes and cannot certify all unexcavated areas. This is a measured architectural comparator within that campaign, without a Copper Scroll site association.
evidence.lineage: Huqoq excavation and 2014–2017 interim report; Wadi Hamam/Qedem Reports 13, Meroth and other inherited campaigns provide comparative material.

evidence.observation: Magness contrasts David and Samson identifications of Meroth’s unlabeled warrior. She favors Alexander and the high priest for Huqoq’s unlabeled elephant panel, while retaining Britt/Boustan’s Antiochus VII–John Hyrcanus interpretation. Notes discuss unresolved details, including a dying bull. Her conclusion surveys varied orientations, benches, entrance relations and floor decoration; notes and cited-source bibliography end at printed 174.
evidence.author_interpretation: She proposes that regional artistic and liturgical preferences better explain diversity than a linear typological sequence, and that some mosaic themes may express local messianic expectations.
evidence.project_inference: Unlabeled image identifications and social meanings are interpretations. Shared figures or classical styles do not identify donor origin, political allegiance or a treasure source. Preserve the printed 360-degree entrance-turn statement as an unresolved angle error.
evidence.lineage: Same Huqoq, Wadi Hamam, Meroth and other field campaigns; competing modern analyses do not add independent objects or observations.

evidence.observation: Ben David distinguishes survey-detectable architectural types from often accidentally excavated types. The native historical count table uses different publication inventories; the 2016 Bornblum source lists 128 sites and the text distinguishes 74 excavated from 54 unexcavated, while its table classifies 88 found by survey and 40 found by excavation.
evidence.author_interpretation: The article argues that detection method affects geographic/type distribution; it notes disputed synagogue identification at Jericho.
evidence.project_inference: Excavation status and discovery method are separate axes:74/54 cannot be substituted for 88/40. These are dated publication inventories, not a verified current landscape denominator. The full article, remaining tables, notes and bibliography are now continuously read through printed 193.
evidence.lineage: Earlier PEF, Sukenik, encyclopedia and Bornblum inventories; avoid counting successive lists as independent field campaigns.

evidence.observation: Ben David’s continuous text distinguishes discovery by survey from later excavation and bases identification on different criteria by period and setting. He would omit Jericho’s proposed early synagogue and Horvat Ethri for lack of benches. Unexcavated categories A–D depend on monumental remains, inscriptions/symbols and inferred regional settlement context. He restricts fragment-only identifications in Byzantine Christian or mixed areas. Some inventory totals disagree internally: Ilan 180/187, early Roman ten/twelve, and table 1’s 1993 discovery-method sum 84 against 77 sites.
evidence.author_interpretation: He attributes part of the geographic distribution to survey visibility, settlement survival and identification rules, and considers benches essential at the present stage of identifying early Roman synagogue buildings.
evidence.project_inference: Detection, eligibility and preservation affect these lists. Criteria tied to assumed regional populations risk becoming circular if used to infer those same populations. The finite published inventory is a useful historical data source; its counts require reconciliation before a regional denominator is adopted.
evidence.lineage: PEF, Kohl/Watzinger, Sukenik, Ilan, TIR, encyclopedias and Bornblum inventories, plus previously reported excavations. Maps replot inherited source data.

evidence.observation: Native figures 1–4 map the inventory, early Roman and Samaritan classes, and discovery by survey versus excavation. Tables 2 and 3 distinguish excavated sites from unexcavated identification categories and retain question marks. The text counts 34 of 74 excavated sites as first detected by survey and 40 only by excavation. For 54 unexcavated sites, categories A–D comprise 3, 26, 7 and 18 sites, with differing material and settlement-context criteria.
evidence.author_interpretation: Ben David attributes part of the geographic and chronological pattern to detection and eligibility criteria and excludes many previously listed architectural-fragment sites. The inventory reflects its publication period.
evidence.project_inference: The table continuation leaves viewer 190 and 192 were absent from the heuristic queue and are now inspected. Discovery mode, excavation status, identification basis and period must remain separate fields. These published lists are unsuitable as a current verified landscape denominator without a fresh source-controlled inventory.
evidence.lineage: Bornblum inventory and inherited surveys/excavations; Dina Shalem’s maps visualize the same list, not an additional field campaign. Full continuous chapter reading, notes and bibliography are complete; see the chapter-specific evidence records.

evidence.observation: Ben David reports 17 synagogue sites among 22 settlement sites in the Upper Galilee survey, 26 among 29 in the western Golan, and 11 among 15 in eastern Galilee. He estimates about 80 percent detection for survey-visible monumental types in these three areas and expressly leaves the detection proportion for randomly excavated types unknown. Tables 2–3 and their continuation leaves, notes and bibliography are read through printed 193; viewer 195 is blank. The prose’s Samaritan and excavated subtype counts differ from table 1 and the total of 74 excavated sites.
evidence.author_interpretation: He expects limited further discoveries of the survey-visible types in those studied rural areas, while advocating more work on early and second–fourth-century synagogues.
evidence.project_inference: Published 54/66 occurrence among surveyed settlement sites is conditional on those survey boundaries and eligibility. It is neither excavation completeness nor an estimated detection probability for all structures. Preserve unknown detection for buried urban, Jordan Valley and earlier buildings.
evidence.lineage: Frankel/Getzov/Aviam/Degani Upper Galilee survey, Ben David Golan survey and Leibner eastern Galilee survey, combined in Bornblum’s dated list; source families overlap existing regional records.

evidence.observation: Tarkhanova traces Capernaum’s excavation and reconstruction history and distinguishes two large carved-frieze groups. She compares their medallion division, linked beads, cornices and carving with Roman and early Byzantine sculpture, mosaics and textiles. The same-piece frieze/cornice and identical cornice decoration are part of her morphological argument. She says the upper-gallery placement originated with Kohl/Watzinger on weak preservation and was repeatedly transmitted without verification. Notes and cited-source bibliography are complete through printed 218; viewers 220–221 are a part divider and blank leaf.
evidence.author_interpretation: She favors late fifth- or sixth-century execution of the friezes by one workshop, possible reuse of stylistically earlier details, and a proposed position over the main colonnades. Both pi-shaped and closed rectangular arrangements remain possible; greater precision requires more investigation.
evidence.project_inference: The essay offers comparative stylistic reasoning and architectural reconstruction. It does not provide a surviving original frieze elevation or a new construction section. Multiple reconstructions, possible spolia and the inferred use of mosaic pattern books remain exploratory. The cited 32 cm Byzantine foot is another scholar’s metrological interpretation, without a new independent measurement here.
evidence.lineage: Kohl/Watzinger, Orfali and Franciscan Capernaum records plus prior publications of comparative monuments and author/Kazaryan photographs; the same stones recur across analyses.

evidence.observation: Native figures show two Capernaum carved-frieze groups, a Moudieleja doorlintel derived from De Vogüé, and a dated church mosaic at Umm al-Rasas. Figure 1 is an A. Kazaryan photograph used by permission; figures 2 and 4 are author photographs. Adjacent text separates observed carving morphology from possible frieze positions.
evidence.author_interpretation: Tarkhanova compares late-antique decorative forms and proposes placing the Capernaum friezes over the main colonnades; she calls the older upper-gallery reconstruction weakly supported and repeatedly transmitted without verification.
evidence.project_inference: Stylistic dating and proposed placement remain interpretations. A photo of relocated stonework cannot supply its original elevation or doorway datum. Preserve permission attribution and keep comparative monuments distinct.
evidence.lineage: Inherited Capernaum remains, De Vogüé illustration and author photography; no new excavation from repetition of the same carving or reconstruction. Full continuous chapter reading, notes and bibliography are complete through printed 218.

evidence.observation: Stern reports 19 inscribed metal sheets on the Maon synagogue apse floor, with others nearby. Only three are described as unrolled, transcribed and published. Published sheets were tightly rolled, one folded; fabric or thread remained on some and one retained a full string. A note allows for additional sheets in private collections and records the author’s uncertainty about later publications.
evidence.author_interpretation: The published inscriptions are interpreted as petitions for healing and protection. The attachment material motivates hypotheses about earlier handling.
evidence.project_inference: This is a potentially useful metal-text deposition comparator, with a restricted published sample and incomplete object history. Floor deposition and a healing interpretation do not establish a hidden treasury, container type or Copper Scroll relationship. The full chapter, notes and bibliography are now read through printed 245; original excavation records remain access leads.
evidence.lineage: Maon excavation finds transmitted through Naveh/Shaked and Bohak publications; Stern’s discussion is derivative of that original object group.

evidence.observation: Stern retains three published Maon/Nirim lamellae from a larger group and sets out competing former-neckwear, suspended display, geniza and post-healing deposit explanations. She says the original deposit mechanism cannot be decided from the available information. A Horvat Kanaf bronze healing text came from fill of building 300 beneath the synagogue; its original context is unknown. At small Baram, the reported bronze lamella was found in situ in a sealed western-stylobate context, with later narrowing of an aisle discussed in note 27.
evidence.author_interpretation: She treats these writings as personal prayers and suggests semi-public display at Maon and possible displacement from the Kanaf synagogue. Those modes and displacement mechanisms are hypotheses.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve floor deposit, sealed architectural deposit and secondary fill as separate contexts. The spatial relation below Kanaf’s synagogue does not prove that the lamella originally belonged to it. Rolled metal texts provide deposition comparanda whose material, purpose and date differ from the Copper Scroll.
evidence.lineage: Maon excavation objects through Naveh/Shaked and Bohak; Kanaf field fill; Aviam’s Baram excavation and Naveh’s text publication. Stern synthesizes these original groups.

evidence.observation: Stern reports a rolled bronze Meroth lamella, 4.8 × 13.8 cm and 26 lines, beneath the stone threshold of the eastern entrance. Note 33 says it was discovered while dismantling the northern wall for adjacent mosaic removal. Note 35 separately reports 485 coins, including 245 gold and the remainder bronze, concealed under a stone with a slot. Her discussion emphasizes that preservation and the rare dismantling of stylobates or thresholds limit detection of embedded texts.
evidence.author_interpretation: She interprets the lamella’s request for dominance over townspeople and its threshold placement as related to their passage above it. She challenges the excavators’ inference that an earlier injustice or founder status explains the commissioner’s conduct.
evidence.project_inference: Threshold location and recovery circumstances are source-reported observations; motive, trampling efficacy and founder access are interpretations. Keep the lamella and separate coin group distinct. Verify original phase, container geometry and retrieval documentation before using the hoard as a concealment model; these figures alone cannot establish a communal treasury.
evidence.lineage: Ilan/Damati Meroth excavation and Naveh/Shaked text publication; the coin and lamella observations share the Meroth campaign already represented elsewhere.

evidence.observation: Stern compares Dura Europos synagogue graffiti with nearby cultic inscriptions and reports clustering on or around doorways. She distinguishes name/remembering texts from monumental donations and stresses that graffiti writers’ biographies and status usually cannot be recovered. Notes cite Dura door-socket tooth/bone deposits and other buried-object studies. The conclusion and full cited-source bibliography are read through printed 245; viewer 247 is blank.
evidence.author_interpretation: She regards many graffiti as prayers whose location and possible vocal reading mattered, and relates individualized inscriptions to varied sacred zones. That interpretation competes with earlier abbreviated-dedication readings.
evidence.project_inference: Text genre, architectural placement and inferred ritual mechanism need separate records. Signature or remembering formulas cannot alone determine social rank or donation. The remarks about abbreviated Greek remembrance do not restart the parked Copper Scroll initials test. Missing embedded objects are sensitive to excavation and preservation opportunities.
evidence.lineage: Yale/French Dura campaigns, Kraeling’s final report, IJO III and earlier Stern analyses; her cross-site argument reuses the same original inscriptions and excavation contexts.

evidence.observation: Ottenheijm/Pater describe Ostia’s possible triclinium and in-situ oven/storage vessels, retaining dating and function uncertainty. They distinguish this room from Jericho’s disputed synagogue identification. Theodotos mentions lodging, rooms and water fittings; dining there is inferred. Stobi and Caesarea inscriptions mention dining space, while the Caesarea building identification is disputed. They compare literary meal references with rabbinic bans and note that the Aramaic phrase can mean upper synagogue rather than an upstairs room.
evidence.author_interpretation: They favor spatially limiting the eating ban to a sacred assembly hall and allowing dining in auxiliary rooms or upper spaces, rather than treating all parts of a complex identically.
evidence.project_inference: Material installations, explicitly inscribed functions and inferred dining must remain distinct. Neither lodging language nor an ambiguous upstairs phrase securely locates a triclinium. Verify the apparent mixed corpus references in notes 7–8 and 20 before citing original object identifiers.
evidence.lineage: Foerster/Ostia, Netzer/Jericho, Theodotos and Stobi/Caesarea inscriptions, rabbinic texts and prior Levine/Habas/Krause analyses; these are inherited observations.

evidence.observation: Ottenheijm/Pater audit smaller columns and proposed stairs. They find no securely related stair remains at Kanaf, En Nashut, Gush Halav, Baram or Hammath Tiberias; several published stairs are conjectural. Capernaum and Chorazin stairs may serve annexes. Shema’s hillside arrangement includes upper western access and a descending southern stair, with a 3 × 7 m gallery reported in note 73. Susiya’s firm upper-space evidence concerns its southern wing. Meroth’s clearest stair remains belong to the late Stage C, although an earlier origin is proposed. Kur’s three-step W7338 platform may lead to a neighboring building or an upper storey.
evidence.author_interpretation: They consider upper levels plausible at several sites but leave their functions uncertain and propose dining, lodging, storage, study or litigation as alternatives to a women’s gallery.
evidence.project_inference: An ascent proves access to something; it does not establish an upper synagogue hall, sex-segregated seating or dining. Separate original stair remains, proposed lost wooden stairs, roof access, annex access and galleries by phase. Architectural alternatives remain conditional until a source plan resolves the connection.
evidence.lineage: Hachlili/Brooten synthesis and original Meiron-project, En Gedi, Susiya, Deir Aziz, Meroth and Horvat Kur reports; the source does not add an independent stair excavation.

evidence.observation: Ottenheijm/Pater compare legal separation of upper rooms and main rooms in inscriptions, Josephus and rabbinic property or meal rulings. Josephus’s anti-theft edict mentions sacred books or funds in synagogue or banquet space; whether these are distinct buildings is debated. They note that going up can be literal or idiomatic entry when rooms share a level. Conclusion, notes and cited-source bibliography end at printed 269; viewer 271 is blank.
