evidence.author_interpretation: They regard communal dining in parts of synagogue complexes as plausible and interpret the rabbinic ban as directed at the assembly hall while upper or auxiliary spaces could have other uses or private status.
evidence.project_inference: Normative legal distinctions and literary rooms do not locate an excavated treasury or establish universal floor arrangements. A mentioned public Roman treasury is the penalty destination in the edict, rather than a Jewish cache location. The proposed explanation remains limited by sparse material evidence.
evidence.lineage: Same synagogue inscriptions and ancient legal/narrative texts with Levine, Habas, Klein and other earlier studies; interpretations are not additional field observations.

evidence.observation: Hakola reports provisional Horvat Kur phases: earlier mosaic floor, second-half-fourth-century attribution with a Constantine coin minted 335–337 in its bedding; replacement broadhouse in the first half of the fifth century; repair and use until late sixth/early seventh. The earlier layout remains unclear. Kur’s named mosaic individual lacks an explicit dedicatory formula. A decorated basalt table is associated with last use. He retains debated Wadi Hamam dates and the Huqoq elephant-panel alternatives. Notes and cited-source bibliography are read through printed 288.
evidence.author_interpretation: He interprets local benefaction and adopted Greek art as ways communities expressed their local identities within wider cultural networks. He warns against making individual donors the sole funding source and acknowledges unresolved resource origins.
evidence.project_inference: The bedding coin is a terminus post quem within the stated context, rather than an exact construction year. Named individuals, costly materials and communal finance models do not locate funds. Imported-pottery ratios may reflect production or detection changes as well as demography. Keep funding, identity and iconographic theories separate from original observations.
evidence.lineage: Horvat Kur/Kinneret Regional Project, Huqoq and Leibner/Wadi Hamam field campaigns plus Lapin’s survey reassessment; reused discoveries and theoretical literature supply the synthesis.

evidence.observation: Spigel’s opening distinguishes unconverted domestic gathering space from a house physically converted into a recognizable communal hall. He defines monumental by designed public use rather than size. He notes that the house-synagogue hypothesis relies heavily on Christian parallels and sparse explicit Jewish literary evidence; he also acknowledges the scarcity and rabbinic selection of those sources. Only the chapter opening is read here; the quantitative analysis begins later.
evidence.author_interpretation: He proposes to test the practical capacity of unconverted houses without claiming that Jews never met in private domestic spaces.
evidence.project_inference: Converted houses and unaltered domestic rooms require separate eligibility. Literary silence cannot certify absence. Quantitative methods, conclusions and bibliography are now continuously read through printed 310; see the capacity and sampling audit.
evidence.lineage: Tsafrir/Miller hypotheses, Dura’s converted building, Christian comparanda and Spigel’s earlier capacity work; no new field observation in these opening pages.

evidence.observation: Spigel compares identified synagogues with the largest covered rooms in a nonexhaustive sample of excavated houses. Kyrios Leontis has a 49 m² room, menorah/ethrog mosaic, community-repair inscription and possible south-wall niche; its model capacity is 58–74. He distinguishes whole-house area from room area, open courtyards, elite triclinia and poorly preserved upper levels. Meiron and Qasrin comparisons use published plans; Qasrin note 37 explicitly contrasts published dimensions with a new scale-plan estimate. Notes and the discussion retain sampling and preservation limits.
evidence.author_interpretation: He regards Kyrios Leontis as a converted house-synagogue and argues that most unconverted domestic rooms offered much less gathering space than monumental synagogues.
evidence.project_inference: Room dimensions and modeled capacity are distinct from actual attendance, original use and settlement population estimates. Sample selection and partial excavation preclude a universal domestic-space denominator. The familiar plans reuse existing campaign observations; comparison with a synagogue from a different century must remain a hypothetical capacity comparison.
evidence.lineage: Bahat/Zori, Meiron project, Qasrin, Sepphoris and Hirschfeld domestic plans; Spigel’s earlier seating methodology, rather than a new excavation or observed attendance count.

evidence.observation: Native figures preserve scaled plans of Kyrios Leontis, Meiron’s domestic industrial complex, Qasrin with nearby houses, Sepphoris’s western summit and the House of Dionysus. Spigel explicitly distinguishes total house area from individual gathering rooms and notes that his survey is not exhaustive. At Qasrin note 37, he contrasts published dimensions of 8 × 2.7 m with a plan-derived estimate closer to 6.3 × 3 m. Printed 300 gives Umm Rihan’s largest room as 41.54 m² alongside 6.7 × 6.5 m, which multiply to 43.55 m².
evidence.author_interpretation: Room areas and a seating coefficient of 0.929 m² per person underpin an argument that most domestic rooms would hold small congregations. Reported capacities are model outputs, not excavated attendance records.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve the explicit Qasrin measurement disagreement and unresolved Umm Rihan arithmetic discrepancy. Plan-based areas, occupied floors, courtyards, upper stories, reconstruction and seating assumptions need distinct provenance; this sample cannot certify the prevalence of domestic worship.
evidence.lineage: Bahat, Meiron-project, Killebrew/Grantham/Fine, Sepphoris and Netzer/Weiss plans reused from prior campaigns; seating estimates derive from Spigel’s previous methodology. Full continuous chapter reading, notes and bibliography are complete; see the chapter-specific evidence records.

evidence.observation: Spigel applies 0.929 m² per person to the eight smallest rooms and obtains 11–26. His synagogue median 261 and mean 333 use upper ends of capacity ranges. He considers larger elite rooms, movable triclinium furnishings, roofs, upper floors and covered peristyles, retaining poor preservation and weather limits. At printed 307 note 75, nonpermanent wood/fabric furnishings are an alternative explanation for absent physical worship alterations. The conclusion and cited-source bibliography are complete through printed 310.
evidence.author_interpretation: He finds widespread domestic worship unlikely as a remedy for the supposed capacity deficit and proposes that many urban Jews may not have participated regularly in communal worship.
evidence.project_inference: The result depends on gathering density, simultaneous attendance, population and household availability assumptions. Lack of permanent furnishings is not a negative excavation test. Actual frequency of worship is not measured by modeled room capacity. Preserve his caveats and alternative spaces instead of treating the domestic hypothesis as archaeologically disproved.
evidence.lineage: Spigel’s prior capacity catalogue and inherited domestic plans, Stobi inscription, rabbinic/Christian parallels and Richardson/Galor interpretations.

evidence.observation: Tervahauta distinguishes wooden Torah arks from architectural shrine structures and says no intact ark/shrine survives. Platforms, niches and apses supply inferred locations; mosaic façades are ambiguous. At Horvat Kur a fifth-century south-wall platform has a north-side staircase and an under-platform interior entered from the east. Its height is estimated at 60–70 cm and its north–south length at about one third of the building. Post-ca. 600 changes filled/lowered it. Umm el-Qanatir has a north-side stair and a small west-side entrance into its platform interior; its gabled aedicula is reconstructed and its date remains uncertain. Meroth’s enlarged western platform is assigned to the early sixth century.
evidence.author_interpretation: She treats Torah-shrine development as parallel with Christian sacred architecture and highlights changing focal areas and communal hierarchy. At Kur architectural fragments suggest columns and a possible roof, rather than a fully preserved superstructure.
evidence.project_inference: The chamber entrances, stairs and platform remains are source-reported architecture; shrine identity, roof, liturgical role and relative chronology are inferences with different confidence. No chamber is turned into a treasury or a scroll target. The proposed Danish mosaic provenance remains unestablished. Original phase plans and excavation records are required before using these chambers as dimensional concealment analogues.
evidence.lineage: Kinneret Regional Project/Kur, Dray–Gonen–Ben David Umm el-Qanatir 2017 preliminary report, Ilan/Damati Meroth and inherited regional campaigns; the same field observations underlie the images and comparisons.

evidence.observation: Native figures show the Hammath Tiberias IIa façade mosaic, an unprovenanced mosaic in Denmark (inventory 15137), and Horvat Kur’s south-side platform after the 2017 season. The Kur caption fixes the photographic viewpoint at the northwest corner. Adjacent text records a north-side stair and an interior space beneath the platform entered from the east. For Denmark’s mosaic, museum correspondence places market acquisition in 1972–1975, while the cited Pentz account assigns a 1975 donation.
evidence.author_interpretation: Tervahauta treats façade imagery as potentially multivalent and ambiguous; Torah-shrine identification, reconstruction of columns/roof and a possible Syrian origin for the Danish mosaic remain interpretation.
evidence.project_inference: Preserve Kur’s excavated access relations independently of the shrine reconstruction. An unprovenanced image supplies no secure place or architectural datum. The apparent missing leading digit in viewer 313’s page header is a pagination anomaly; readable body text remains available. Full chapter, notes and bibliography are now continuously read through printed 336; see the qualified chamber-function discussion.
evidence.lineage: Dothan’s Hammath campaign, Denmark museum collection history and Kinneret Regional Project 2017 Kur observations; images and subsequent interpretations share those source families.

evidence.observation: Tervahauta reviews uneven literary and archaeological evidence for sanctity, Jewish/Christian interaction and gender/authority. She warns that elite prescriptive sources do not describe all ordinary practice, symbols do not settle identities, and attendance was not universal. At printed 331 she states that the exact use of Kur and Umm el-Qanatir under-platform spaces is unknown; valuable-object storage and genizot are possibilities. Note 84 points to the excavators’ geniza interpretation for both the platform chamber and the larger space under the western aisle at Umm el-Qanatir. The conclusion, notes and full cited-source bibliography end at printed 336; viewers 338–339 are a part divider and blank.
evidence.author_interpretation: She proposes that storage of valued sacred objects might enhance holiness, analogously to Christian relics beneath altars, and favors negotiation/hybridity over a single rivalry model. She hypothesizes access restrictions and hierarchies without identifying who used the platform or chamber.
evidence.project_inference: Possible geniza, valuable-object storage, relic analogy and restricted access remain interpretations. Do not substitute them for recovered contents or a demonstrable deposit. Spatial hierarchy and communal funding explain neither a concealed treasury nor treasure survival. Religious/political causal theories are attributed to the author and do not add archaeological observations.
evidence.lineage: The same Kur and Umm el-Qanatir campaigns, rabbinic/Christian literary traditions and Fine, Habas, Milson, Yasin and other interpretive scholarship.

evidence.observation: Weiss surveys synagogue mosaic layouts and examines Wadi Hamam, Sepphoris and En Gedi in detail. Figure 1 is an expressly suggested Wadi Hamam reconstruction; surviving aisle fragments and the proposed nave circle are distinguished. Sepphoris figure 2 preserves the building plan. En Gedi figure 3 shows the mosaic from above, with geometric panels, birds/peacocks and the west-aisle inscription. He corrects a Temple-construction reading of a Wadi Hamam scene to Tower of Babel. He retains the Wadi Hamam/Huqoq chronology dispute and says a shared earlier iconographic source cannot be proved. Conclusion and cited-source bibliography are complete through printed 354.
evidence.author_interpretation: He proposes longer Wadi Hamam use than the excavator’s mid-fourth-century abandonment, a partly urban-to-rural development of polemical mosaic programs, and possible communal compromise, cost or artisan availability behind En Gedi’s layout.
evidence.project_inference: Observed tesserae, proposed panel reconstruction, chronological argument and political/artistic interpretation remain separate. Simpler art does not measure community finances. Weiss’s printed 349 statement linking Jericho’s nonfigural floor to the rise of Islam differs from Magness’s caution at printed 162 that last-use coins do not date the beginning; preserve both author positions. These are exploratory syntheses of exposed campaigns.
evidence.lineage: Leibner/Miller Wadi Hamam, Weiss/Netzer Sepphoris, Barag/Porat/Netzer En Gedi, Huqoq and other inherited campaigns; Porat’s final report is cited as forthcoming in the volume.

evidence.observation: Native figure 1 overlays surviving Khirbet Wadi Hamam mosaic fragments on a proposed complete prayer-hall scheme with north arrow, 10 m scale and numbered aisle panels.
evidence.author_interpretation: The caption expressly calls this a suggested reconstruction. Adjacent text tentatively calls the nave circle a zodiac and dates the later mosaic to the late third or early fourth century CE.
evidence.project_inference: Keep preserved tesserae and proposed infill separate. Reconstructed panel positions and a probable zodiac are unsuitable as measured architectural or iconographic observations without their original evidentiary basis. Full chapter, notes and bibliography are now continuously read through printed 354.
evidence.lineage: Leibner’s Wadi Hamam campaign; B. Arubas and M. Edelcopp reconstruction. Repeated illustration shares the underlying excavation already in Source 58.

evidence.observation: Native figure 2 shows the Sepphoris building and mosaic compartments without a printed scale or north arrow. Figure 3 is an overhead En Gedi mosaic photograph credited to Zev Radovan/Center for Jewish Art, with the small platform-side mosaic and west-aisle band included.
evidence.author_interpretation: Weiss uses these mosaics to compare arrangements and viewing direction; their economic and polemical causes are proposed explanations.
evidence.project_inference: The unscaled schematic and unrectified overhead photograph do not supply surveyed coordinates or precise dimensions. Keep the north-aisle orientation from the text separate from inferred directions in an unlabelled picture.
evidence.lineage: Weiss/Netzer Sepphoris campaign and Barag/Porat/Netzer En Gedi, with Center for Jewish Art photography; no new field observation.

evidence.observation: Xeravits reviews Japhi’a’s secondary lintels and Sukenik’s excavation. Only one and a half medallions survive from a reconstructed twelve around concentric circles of 3.8 and 1.9 m. The second animal and fragmentary inscription allow competing tribe and zodiac readings, with final mem/samekh uncertain. Figure 1 is a derivative reconstruction; figure 2 preserves the animal/inscription photograph. The eleventh-century Saint Catherine manuscript in figure 3 is a later comparator. He audits horn form, calendar layout, corner imagery, textual chronology and non-Jewish parallels. Conclusion, memorial note and bibliography are complete through printed 365; viewer 367 is blank.
evidence.author_interpretation: He favors a zodiac possibility over a twelve-tribe model but says the inscription cannot be securely read from present preservation or available photographs. The interpretation requires further research.
evidence.project_inference: The reconstructed medallion count, animal identification and restored name are not preserved complete observations. Later manuscript and midrash parallels do not date the mosaic; no epigraphic certainty or original photogrammetric dimensions are supplied. This does not reopen any manuscript-letter test or locate a Copper Scroll landmark.
evidence.lineage: Vincent secondary-find account, Sukenik 1951 preliminary excavation report, Hachlili synthesis, Center for Jewish Art photo and comparative mosaic/manuscript publications; no new Japhi’a excavation.

evidence.observation: Individual native review covers Japhi’a’s opening, the derivative Hachlili mosaic drawing and preserved animal/inscription photograph, plus the later Saint Catherine manuscript comparator. Captions, the author’s final-letter uncertainty and the public-domain label for the LOC manuscript photo are preserved. Viewer 359 renders its header as 58 rather than 358.
evidence.author_interpretation: The drawing and manuscript comparison support the author’s iconographic discussion; neither resolves the uncertain inscription.
evidence.project_inference: Do not read the damaged name from a low-resolution article photograph as a secure epigraphic observation. Archive original attribution and keep late comparanda separate from the ancient mosaic.
evidence.lineage: Sukenik Japhi’a/Hachlili derivative drawing, Center for Jewish Art photograph and LOC Saint Catherine manuscript image.

evidence.observation: Chakovskaya reassesses Beth Alpha’s mosaic using composition, text, tesserae/color production, body proportions, artist inscription terminology and Coptic textiles. Figures show a modified Sukenik mosaic plate and museum textile comparanda. She cites average tessera density 100/dm² (186/dm² for figures) and twenty-one colors through Merrony; these are inherited values. Greek technitai versus psēphothetēs counts come from an online inscription search with stated stems but no frozen corpus/date. She acknowledges a sculptor/stone-carver origin as a hypothesis; stylistic comparison does not identify the artists’ birthplace. Conclusion and bibliography end at printed 392.
evidence.author_interpretation: She argues that flatness, omission, outline and color may be deliberate expressive choices rather than failed naturalism and proposes possible stone-carver training and a surrounding Coptic artistic milieu.
evidence.project_inference: Style, production quality and dating need separate evidence. Modern artist opinion, lexical frequencies and body ratios do not establish training or migration. A zodiac Aquarius image interpreted as a well/cistern is iconographic imagery rather than a surveyed installation. Preserved art and modified illustrations remain separate; no architectural cache measurement is added.
evidence.lineage: Sukenik Beth Alpha campaign, Zohar production study, Merrony catalogue, PHI corpus search and museum textiles; artistic reassessment reuses the same monuments and published objects.

evidence.observation: Native figure 1 is expressly modified after Sukenik plate XXVII and preserves gaps in the Beth Alpha mosaic. Figure 2 gives the Metropolitan Museum textile accession 90.5.848, dimensions 23.5 × 25 cm and CC0; figure 3 gives Brooklyn Museum accession 42.438.4, 24 × 24 cm and CC-BY. The adjacent Beth Alpha compositional and Coptic-school pages are individually inspected. Viewer 373 renders its header as 72 rather than 372.
evidence.author_interpretation: Chakovskaya compares contours, color and abstraction and proposes intentional composition and possible Coptic connections.
evidence.project_inference: Museum textile licences are caption-specific, not permission for the entire modern article. Modified mosaic illustration, actual preservation and artistic interpretation remain separate. These textile comparisons add no architectural cache observation.
evidence.lineage: Sukenik Beth Alpha plate and museum objects, with modern reinterpretation; same underlying archaeological and collection records.

evidence.observation: Gilbert reviews early and late menorah images, noting sparse pre-70 material, uncertain ossuary dates and Magdala’s public stone exception. Temple vessels in Rome derive mainly from Josephus, rabbinic memories and later contested traditions. He states that the fate of the Temple of Peace contents after the 192 CE fire is unreported and that Procopius’s later stories are unverifiable. Printed 403 distinguishes 2 Baruch’s literary concealment narrative from the Roman display account and labels the modern Jerusalem-return hypothesis speculative. He notes no direct contemporary report of Jews’ reactions and the absence of a menorah from Bar Kokhba coinage. The conclusion and complete bibliography end at printed 411.
evidence.author_interpretation: He proposes that Jews’ expanded visual use of the menorah partly reclaimed a sacred object from Roman triumphal ideology, alongside other explanations. He does not claim that every depiction conveyed resistance.
evidence.project_inference: Actual finds, literary testimony, later memory and modern causal reconstruction remain separate. 2 Baruch, Benjamin of Tudela and Procopius do not provide located archaeological deposits or evidence for surviving Temple objects. Do not equate pictured/remembered vessels with a Copper Scroll inventory or infer custody after the fire. Rare-image survival and symbolic frequency do not measure the whole ancient population’s beliefs.
evidence.lineage: Hasmonean coin corpus, Rahmani/Geva Jerusalem finds, Magdala campaign, Dura and later synagogue observations; Josephus and literary traditions interpreted through Fine, Boustan, Noy, Chapman and others.

evidence.observation: The complete index and author biographies are read. Index entries include archaeology, synagogues, lamellae, ritual baths, shrine platforms, dining, identity and iconography. Several index ranges are inconsistent with the actual chapter pagination: menorah points to 408–419 although Gilbert’s essay is printed 393–411; Japhi’a points to 363–369 although Xeravits’s essay is printed 355–365; the synagogue-art peopled-scrolls range extends to 228 beyond Tarkhanova’s chapter end 218. The biographies end at printed 419, the last PDF leaf.
evidence.author_interpretation: The index offers thematic access and the biographies describe contributors’ roles at publication; neither supplies additional archaeological evidence.
evidence.project_inference: Retrieve citations using the body’s printed pages and verified viewer mapping rather than an unverified index pointer. Biographies are publication-time metadata, not current appointment checks. Full available source text, notes, per-chapter bibliographies and back matter are complete; native figure and integrity closure is recorded separately.
evidence.lineage: The same 2021 proceedings and its editorial index; no independent field observation from indexing or author credentials.

evidence.observation: The native final index leaf is inspected in full, including its two columns. The peopled-scrolls range is visibly printed as 215–228, confirming that the inaccurate range is in the supplied source rather than an extraction error.
evidence.author_interpretation: The index is an editorial retrieval aid.
evidence.project_inference: Use body-page citations and campaign lineage instead of treating erroneous index ranges as source evidence.
evidence.lineage: Editorial back matter of the same 2021 proceedings.
